source_text: Ἅπαν γὰρ εἶδος ἐπῆλθε τρυφῆς, καὶ ψυχαγωγίας παντοδαποὺς ἐπενόησε τρόπους, καὶ ποικίλας καὶ πολυτρόπους τέρψεων εὗρεν ἰδέας, καὶ ταύτας δι ηγούμενος ἔλεγεν· Ὠκοδόμησά μοι οἴκους, ἐφύτευσά μοι ἀμπελῶνας, ἐποίησά μοι κήπους καὶ παραδείσους, ἐποίησά μοι κολυμβήθρας ὑδάτων, ἐκτησάμην δούλους καὶ παιδίσκας, καὶ οἰκογενεῖς ἐγένοντό μοι· κτῆσις βουκολίων καὶ ποιμνίων ἐγένετό μοι· συνήγαγον ἀργύριον καὶ χρυσίον ἴσα ψάμμῳ· ἐποίησά μοι ᾄδοντας καὶ ᾀδούσας, οἰνοχόους καὶ οἰνοχοούσας. Τί οὖν ὁ αὐτὸς οὗτος μετὰ τοσαύτην περιουσίαν τῶν χρημάτων, τῶν κτη μάτων, τῆς τρυφῆς, τῆς ἀνέσεως; Ἐμακάρισα, φησὶ, τοὺς ἀποθανόντας ὑπὲρ τοὺς ζῶντας, καὶ ἀγαθὸς ὑπὲρ τούτους ὅστις οὔπω ἐγένετο. Ὄντως ἀξιόπιστος οὗτος κατήγορος τρυφῆς, ὁ τοιαῦτα περὶ αὐτῆς ψηφιζόμενος. Εἰ μὲν γάρ τις τῶν ἐν πενίᾳ καὶ πτωχείᾳ βεβιωκότων ταύτην ἐξέφερε τὴν ψῆφον κατὰ τῆς τρυφῆς, ἔδοξεν ἂν οὐκ ἀληθείᾳ, ἀλλ' ἀπειρίᾳ ταῦτα κατηγορεῖν· ὅταν δὲ ὁ πᾶσαν αὐτὴν ἐπελθὼν καὶ διερευνησάμενος αὐτῆς ἑκάστην ὁδὸν, οὗτος αὐ τὴν ἀτιμάζῃ, ἀνύποπτος ἡ κατηγορία λοιπόν. Τάχα νομίζετε τῆς παρούσης ὑποθέσεως ἡμῖν ἐκπεπτωκέναι τὸν λόγον· ἀλλ' εἴπερ προσέχωμεν, εὑρήσομεν, ὅτι ταύτης μάλιστα ἔχεται τὰ εἰρημένα. Ἐν γὰρ μαρτύρων μνείαις ἀναγκαῖον καὶ ἀκόλουθον, καὶ τοὺς περὶ φιλοσοφίας κινεῖν λόγους. Καὶ ταῦτα λέγομεν οὐ τῆς παρούσης κατηγοροῦντες ζωῆς, μὴ γένοιτο, ἀλλὰ τὴν τρυφὴν διαβάλλοντες· οὐ γὰρ τὸ ζῇν κακὸν, ἀλλὰ τὸ εἰκῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς ζῇν. βʹ. Ὡς ἐάν τις ἐπὶ κατορθώμασι καὶ τῇ τῶν μελλόν των ἀγαθῶν ἐλπίδι τὸν παρόντα ζήσῃ βίον, δυνήσεται κατὰ Παῦλον λέγειν, ὅτι Τὸ ζῇν ἐν σαρκὶ πολλῷ κρεῖσσον· τοῦτο γὰρ καρπὸς ἔργου· καθά περ οὖν καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ μακαρίου γέγονεν Εὐσταθίου, ὃς καὶ τῇ ζωῇ καὶ τῇ τελευτῇ πρὸς τὸ δέον ἐχρήσατο. Οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκείας γῆς, ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τῆς ἀλλοτρίας ταύτην ὑπέμεινε διὰ τὸν Χριστόν· τοῦτο τῶν ἐχθρῶν τὸ κατόρθωμα. Ἐκεῖνοι μὲν γὰρ τῆς πατρίδος αὐτὸν ἐξήλασαν ὡς ἀτιμάζοντες· ὁ δὲ λαμπρότερος ἐγίνετο μᾶλλον καὶ περιφανέστερος τῇ πρὸς τὴν ὑπερορίαν μεταστάσει, ὡς καὶ τῶν πραγμάτων τὸ τέλος ἀπέδειξε. Τοσαύτη γὰρ ἡ περιφάνεια γέγονεν, ὡς τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ ταφέντος ἐν Θρᾴκῃ, τὴν μνήμην αὐτοῦ καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν παρ' ἡμῖν ἀν θεῖν, καὶ τὸν μὲν τάφον εἶναι ἐν ἐκείνῳ τῷ βαρβα ρικῷ χωρίῳ, τὸν δὲ πόθον παρ' ἡμῖν, τοῖς ἐκ τοσού του ἀπειργομένοις διαστήματος, μετὰ χρόνον τοσοῦ τον καθ' ἑκάστην αὔξεσθαι τὴν ἡμέραν· μᾶλλον δὲ, εἰ χρὴ τἀληθὲς εἰπεῖν, καὶ ὁ τάφος αὐτοῦ παρ' ἡμῖν, οὐκ ἐν Θρᾴκῃ μόνον. Μνήματα γὰρ ἁγίων οὐ σοροὶ, καὶ λάρνακες, καὶ στῆλαι, καὶ γράμματα, ἀλλ' ἔρ γων κατορθώματα, καὶ πίστεως ζῆλος, καὶ συνειδὸς πρὸς Θεὸν ὑγιές. Καὶ γὰρ πάσης στήλης λαμπροτέρα ἀνέστηκεν αὕτη ἡ Ἐκκλησία τῷ μάρτυρι, γράμματα ἔχουσα οὐκ ἄφωνα, ἀλλὰ διὰ τῶν πραγμάτων αὐτῶν λαμπρότερον σάλπιγγος βοῶντα τὴν ἐκείνου μνήμην καὶ τὴν λαμπρότητα, καὶ ἕκαστος ὑμῶν τῶν παρ όντων τοῦ ἁγίου τάφος ἐστὶν ἐκείνου, τάφος ἔμψυχος καὶ πνευματικός. Ἂν γὰρ ἀναπτύξω τὸ συνειδὸς ἑκάστου τῶν παρόντων ὑμῶν, εὑρίσκω τὸν ἅγιον τοῦτον ἔνδον τῆς διανοίας ὑμῶν ἐνδιαιτώμενον.
thought_title: Solomon condemns luxury; Eustathius' living tomb
orientation: Chrysostom is arguing that martyrdom is determined by intention, and he has just introduced Solomon as a witness who called the dead blessed; now he quotes Solomon's own account of his luxury and applies it to Eustathius' exile and enduring memory.
pass_a_gloss: For every form of luxury came upon him, and he devised manifold modes of diversion, and he found varied and many-shaped forms of pleasures, and recounting these he said: I built for myself houses, I planted for myself vineyards, I made for myself gardens and parks, I made for myself pools of waters, I acquired male slaves and female slaves, and home-born slaves became mine; a possession of herds and flocks became mine; I gathered silver and gold equal to sand; I made for myself male singers and female singers, male cupbearers and female cupbearers. What then did this same man say after so great an abundance of money, of possessions, of luxury, of ease? I counted blessed, he says, the dead above the living, and good above these is whoever has not yet come into being. Truly this man is a trustworthy accuser of luxury, he who casts such a vote about it. For if one of those who had lived in poverty and beggary had brought forth this vote against luxury, he would have seemed to accuse these things not by truth but by inexperience; but when the one who went through all of it and searched out each of its paths, this man dishonors it, the accusation is henceforth beyond suspicion. Perhaps you think that our discourse has fallen away from the present subject; but if we pay attention, we will find that what has been said especially holds to this subject. For in commemorations of martyrs it is necessary and fitting also to stir up discourses about virtuous life. And we say these things not accusing the present life, may it never be, but slandering luxury; for living is not evil, but living idly and simply is evil. 2. As if someone lives the present life in good deeds and in hope of the good things to come, he will be able to say with Paul, that To live in the flesh is far better; for this is fruit of work; just as indeed it also happened in the case of the blessed Eustathius, who used both his life and his death for what was fitting. For not on his own land, but on foreign land he endured this death for Christ; this was the achievement of his enemies. For those men drove him out of his fatherland as if dishonoring him; but he became more splendid rather and more distinguished by his removal to exile, as also the end of the events showed. For so great was the distinction that, although his body was buried in Thrace, his memory blooms among us each day, and the tomb is in that barbarian place, but the longing is among us, who are separated by so great a distance, and after so great a time it increases each day; rather, if one must speak the truth, his tomb is also among us, not only in Thrace. For memorials of saints are not coffins, and chests, and pillars, and inscriptions, but achievements of deeds, and zeal of faith, and a conscience sound toward God. For this church has arisen as a monument to the martyr brighter than every pillar, having letters not voiceless, but through the deeds themselves crying out more brightly than a trumpet his memory and his splendor, and each of you who are present is a tomb of the saint, a living and spiritual tomb. For if I unfold the conscience of each of you who are present, I find this saint dwelling within your mind.

choices.why: Glossary term; renders the self-indulgent softness Solomon describes, not mere pleasure.
Glossary term for the specific suffering Eustathius endured for Christ.
Keeps the paradox of the metaphor: the hearers themselves are tombs that are alive.
Renders the successful deed; here used ironically of the enemies' success in exiling Eustathius.
Preserves the forensic force of Solomon as accuser of luxury.
rejected: the accusation is free from suspicion

bible_refs.note: I built for myself houses, I planted for myself vineyards, I made for myself gardens and parks, I made for myself pools of waters, I acquired male slaves and female slaves, and home-born slaves became mine; a possession of herds and flocks became mine; I gathered silver and gold equal to sand; I made for myself male singers and female singers, male cupbearers and female cupbearers.
I counted blessed the dead above the living, and good above these is whoever has not yet come into being.
To live in the flesh is far better; for this is fruit of work.

pass_b_english: Every form of luxury came his way, and he devised all kinds of diversions. He discovered varied and manifold forms of enjoyment, and as he described them he said: “I built for myself houses, I planted for myself vineyards, I made for myself gardens and parks, I made for myself pools of water, I acquired male and female slaves, and home-born slaves became mine. I possessed herds and flocks. I gathered silver and gold equal to sand. I made for myself male and female singers, male and female cupbearers” (Ecclesiastes 2:4-8). What then did this same man say after such abundance of wealth, possessions, luxury, and ease? “I counted the dead blessed above the living,” he said, “and better than both is the one who has not yet come into being” (Ecclesiastes 4:2). Truly this man is a trustworthy accuser of luxury, since he passes such a judgment on it. If someone who had lived in poverty and want had brought this verdict against luxury, he would seem to accuse it not from truth but from inexperience. But when the man who explored all of it and searched out every one of its paths dishonors it, the accusation is beyond suspicion.

Perhaps you think our discourse has wandered from the present subject. But if we pay attention, we will find that what has been said is closely tied to it. For in commemorations of martyrs it is necessary and fitting to stir up words about the virtuous life as well. And we say these things not to accuse the present life—God forbid—but to discredit luxury. For living is not evil, but living carelessly and without purpose is.

If someone lives this present life with good deeds and the hope of the good things to come, he will be able to say with Paul, “To live in the flesh is far better; for this is the fruit of work” (Philippians 1:22). This is what happened with the blessed Eustathius, who used both his life and his death as he ought. For he endured this not on his own soil but on foreign soil, for Christ's sake. This was the achievement of his enemies. They drove him from his homeland as if to dishonor him, but he became more brilliant and more distinguished by his removal into exile, as the outcome of events proved. So great was his distinction that although his body was buried in Thrace, his memory blooms among us every day. The tomb is in that barbarian place, but the longing is here among us, separated by so great a distance, and after so much time it grows with each passing day. Or rather, to speak the truth, his tomb is also among us, not only in Thrace. For the memorials of the saints are not coffins, chests, pillars, and inscriptions, but achievements of deeds, zeal for the faith, and a conscience sound before God. This church has risen up as a monument to the martyr more brilliant than any pillar, bearing inscriptions that are not silent but proclaim his memory and his splendor through the very facts more loudly than a trumpet. And each one of you here present is that saint's tomb—a living and spiritual tomb. For if I unfold the conscience of each one of you here present, I find this holy man dwelling within your mind.

problems.quote: he endured his death not on his own soil but on foreign soil
problems.source_quote: Οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκείας γῆς, ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τῆς ἀλλοτρίας ταύτην ὑπέμεινε διὰ τὸν Χριστόν
problems.why: ταύτην refers back to τὴν ζωήν (life) from the previous clause, not τὴν τελευτήν (death). Eustathius endured his *life* in exile, not his death. The English 'death' contradicts the source which emphasizes he used both life and death well, but specifically endured exile during his life.
problems.fix: he endured this not on his own soil but on foreign soil

edits.old: For he endured his death not on his own soil but on foreign soil, for Christ's sake.
edits.new: For he endured this not on his own soil but on foreign soil, for Christ's sake.

fixed: Changed 'his death' to 'this' because ταύτην refers back to τὴν ζωήν (life) from the previous clause, not to death. Eustathius endured his life in exile, not his death.

last_rejected.quote: What then did this same man say after such abundance of wealth, possessions, luxury, and ease?
last_rejected.source_quote: Τί οὖν ὁ αὐτὸς οὗτος μετὰ τοσαύτην περιουσίαν τῶν χρημάτων, τῶν κτημάτων, τῆς τρυφῆς, τῆς ἀνέσεως;
last_rejected.why: Source has no verb 'say'; it asks 'what about this man after such abundance?' The added verb slightly changes sense.
last_rejected.fix: What then about this same man after such abundance of wealth, possessions, luxury, and ease?
last_rejected.ruling: Greek τί + question mark implies 'what [did he say/do]'; 'say' is natural inference from following ἔφησι quotation, not meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: To live in the flesh is far better; for this is the fruit of work
last_rejected.source_quote: Τὸ ζῇν ἐν σαρκὶ πολλῷ κρεῖσσον· τοῦτο γὰρ καρπὸς ἔργου
last_rejected.why: Paul's Greek says 'far better' (πολλῷ κρεῖσσον) but the context in Philippians 1:22 is about fruitful labor, not 'work' generally. More critically, the English omits that this is a conditional or concessive sense—Paul says living in the flesh is better *because* it means fruitful labor for Christ. The English 'fruit of work' is vague and loses the specific sense of 'fruitful labor' or 'fruit of my work.'
last_rejected.fix: 'To live in the flesh is far better'—for this means fruitful labor. This is what happened with the blessed Eustathius
last_rejected.ruling: καρπὸς ἔργου = 'fruit of work'; Pauline nuance is implicit. Not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: This was the achievement of his enemies
last_rejected.why: The Greek says 'this was the enemies' achievement/success'—but the context shows this is bitter irony. The enemies *thought* they succeeded by exiling him, but actually glorified him. The English 'achievement' reads as straight praise of the enemies, missing the ironic force that their 'success' backfired.
last_rejected.fix: This was the enemies' 'triumph'—or rather, their intended defeat of him became his glory
last_rejected.ruling: κατόρθωμα = 'achievement/success'; irony is clear from context. Normal rendering range, not misleading.
